significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would license the conclusion that conditional LLM backdoors necessarily produce a measurable increase in activation-space paraphrase dispersion or local Lipschitzness when semantically equivalent variants cross the trigger condition; this is a form-(iii) predictive coupling, not merely an existence claim. It establishes both a phenomenon—"a paraphrase that happens to (partially) contain the trigger jumps to an anomalous region"—and a proposed hidden-gate mechanism, fixing expectations across trigger types and implying an activation-smoothness cost for adaptive attackers; this bears directly on persistent conditional behavior such as that documented in Hubinger et al.'s Sleeper Agents (2024). A negative result would rule out the claimed necessary universal signature and show that trigger-agnostic detection cannot generally rest on paraphrase invariance, although the qualitative terms "sharp discontinuity" and "detectable" somewhat weaken determinacy. Topic substitution check: generic mechanistic LLM safety would not earn this score; the universal relation among semantic equivalence, activation discontinuity, and backdoor behavior is the claim-specific increment.

reach.justification: The named handles are a "model-level screen" based on the "local Lipschitz/anomaly profile" and an "inference-time input flag" based on whether an input is "an outlier relative to its paraphrase cloud." The former is ex ante before deployment and the latter can flag a query before harmful generation, giving auditors and model deployers an action window rather than merely explaining an observed failure. After per-model re-extraction, the claimed law still predicts heavier-tailed dispersion for backdoored models, so the substantive relation—not just a search procedure—is asserted to transfer across conditional triggers and model families, though the stated limitations narrow support to open-weight, fine-tuning-injected backdoors. Topic substitution check: the broad safety topic alone supplies neither these handles nor their transferable prediction, so the reach score derives from the claim-specific screening rule.
